tagline: Follow the Teche past bayou crossings, cane baskets and plantation houses
intro: The Bayou Teche Byway follows the slow-moving bayou west of the Atchafalaya Basin, linking towns in St. Martin, Iberia and St. Mary parishes. Louisiana’s tourism office suggests half a day to two days for a self-guided tour. National Scenic Byway designation followed in 2021; the state’s announcement emphasizes food, music, art and crafts passed between generations along the route.

Before the driving route, the Teche served as the principal transportation corridor for the eighteenth-century Acadian migration into this region. Crossings helped settlements grow: at Breaux Bridge, an 1817 wagon bridge replaced the earlier footbridge and supported commerce. After the Louisiana Purchase, Anglo settlers established sugar plantations along the bayou. At Shadows-on-the-Teche, that economy depended on enslaved people. Logging drew workers into the Atchafalaya Basin, where cypress supplied lumber for houses and businesses. Oil and gas later brought offshore work. The tourism office includes the Cypress Sawmill Museum and Morgan City’s Mr. Charlie oil rig among places interpreting these changes.

For a southbound journey, begin at Arnaudville, where Bayou Teche meets Bayou Fusilier. Continue through Breaux Bridge and St. Martinville toward New Iberia and Shadows-on-the-Teche. Farther down the bayou, Charenton is home to the Chitimacha reservation and museum; Franklin and Morgan City complete the journey.

moments.title: Breaux Bridge
moments.text: The town’s name began as a direction to a crossing. Firmin Breaux built a footbridge over the Teche in 1799 for family and neighbors. It was a suspension bridge, tied to pilings and large live oaks on both banks. In 1817, Agricole and Scholastique Breaux replaced it with a bridge that carried wagons. After Agricole died, Scholastique drew a town plan and sold lots to other Acadian settlers, founding Breaux Bridge in 1829. Her plan included both a detailed map of the area and a diagram setting out the town’s streets. The community holds an annual Crawfish Festival.

moments.title: Shadows-on-the-Teche
moments.text: Eight white-plastered brick columns front the handmade red brick house at Shadows-on-the-Teche. The columns stand on high square bases and support the upper gallery, with a Doric frieze above. Built in 1834 for David and Mary Conrad Weeks, it was designed as a town house for social life and entertainment. The household depended on enslaved labor, and David’s will left 164 enslaved people to his children. In 1958, William Weeks Hall donated the house and garden to the National Trust for Historic Preservation. The Iberia African American Historical Society opened a research and learning center here in 2022.
moments.notice: The eight Tuscan columns are white-plastered brick, set against the house’s red brick construction.

moments.title: Charenton
moments.text: Charenton is home to a Chitimacha community and reservation museum. Chitimacha women continue weaving rivercane baskets, typically using yellow, red and black. Women also called for help when unpaid taxes threatened the tribe’s remaining land. Sarah Avery McIlhenney responded by purchasing land at a sheriff’s sale in 1915; it subsequently entered federal trust for the tribe. Present cultural work includes language immersion classes and a project encouraging river cane regrowth to support basket weaving. The tribe uses linguist Morris Swadesh’s notes and recordings to help revitalize its language, with teaching for children and adults as well as materials for home use.
